expectedText:
LATE FEES ON RESIDENTIAL RENT AS LIQUIDATED DAMAGES (CIV. CODE §§ 1671(D), 1951.5) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 · Pat Morgan

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes how California law treats a late fee charged on residential rent — a contractual charge a tenant owes when rent is paid after its due date — as it may bear on the tenancy of Jordan Lee at 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 under a rental agreement with Pat Morgan. It states what Civil Code sections 1671 and 1951.5 provide, what California courts have said about when such a charge is enforceable and when it is a void penalty, what a landlord may recover as actual damages when a late-fee clause is void, what Code of Civil Procedure section 1161 requires a three-day notice for nonpayment to state, and what Civil Code section 1719 provides about a service charge on a dishonored check. It does not determine whether any particular late fee, rental agreement term, or notice concerning 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 is valid, and it does not tell Pat Morgan or Jordan Lee what to do about any charge or dispute.

LIQUIDATED DAMAGES IN A LEASE OF A DWELLING: CIVIL CODE SECTIONS 1951.5 AND 1671(C)-(D)
A late fee in a residential rental agreement is a contractual provision fixing in advance what the tenant owes for a breach — paying rent late — so California's liquidated damages statute governs it. Civil Code section 1951.5 states that section 1671, relating to liquidated damages, applies to a lease of real property. Section 1671 then divides liquidated damages provisions into two tracks. Under subdivision (b), the general rule for contracts is that such a provision is valid unless the party attacking it shows it was unreasonable when the contract was made. Subdivision (c)(2) removes a lease of real property for use as a dwelling by the tenant, or by those dependent on the tenant for support, from that general rule: for such a lease, validity is determined under subdivision (d) and not under subdivision (b). Subdivision (d) states that in those cases the provision is void, except that the parties may agree on an amount presumed to be the damage sustained by the breach when, from the nature of the case, it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage. The statutory default for a dwelling lease is therefore the opposite of the general contract default: the clause is void unless the impracticability condition is satisfied, rather than valid unless shown unreasonable.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Section 1671, relating to liquidated damages, applies to a lease of real property."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1951.5, California Civil Code, liquidated damages statute applied to leases of real property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1951.5.)
  "Except as provided in subdivision (c), a provision in a contract liquidating the damages for the breach of the contract is valid unless the party seeking to invalidate the provision establishes that the provision was unreasonable under the circumstances existing at the time the contract was made."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1671(b), California Civil Code, the general rule for liquidated damages provisions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1671.)
  "The validity of a liquidated damages provision shall be determined under subdivision (d) and not under subdivision (b) where the liquidated damages are sought to be recovered from either: ... (2) A party to a lease of real property for use as a dwelling by the party or those dependent upon the party for support."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1671(c), California Civil Code, dwelling leases routed to subdivision (d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1671.)
  "In the cases described in subdivision (c), a provision in a contract liquidating damages for the breach of the contract is void except that the parties to such a contract may agree therein upon an amount which shall be presumed to be the amount of damage sustained by a breach thereof, when, from the nature of the case, it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1671(d), California Civil Code, void except on a showing of impracticability (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1671.)
  Known gap: Section 1671 does not use the words "late fee," "late charge," or "rent"; the application of subdivisions (c)(2) and (d) to a residential late-rent charge comes from the courts described in the other clauses of this sheet, not from the section's own text. Section 1671(c)(1) separately covers retail purchases or rentals of personal property or services for personal, family, or household purposes and is not quoted here. Section 1671 has not been amended since 1977 and section 1951.5 since 1977; neither the 1977 legislation nor its legislative history was fetched. This sheet does not address commercial leases, to which subdivision (b) rather than subdivision (d) applies, and it does not address whether a particular unit at 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 is used as a dwelling within subdivision (c)(2).

WHO MUST PROVE WHAT: OROZCO V. CASIMIRO AND DEL MONTE PROPERTIES V. DOLAN
Two published California appellate division decisions have applied section 1671(d) to a residential late fee, and both placed the burden on the landlord. In Orozco v. Casimiro (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th Supp. 7, a landlord's unlawful detainer case rested on a $50 late fee in a lease. The court described the tenant's contention as being that the landlord must plead and prove that damages were impracticable or extremely difficult to fix. It held that once a landlord makes that showing, the agreed amount is presumed to represent the damage suffered — but the landlord there had neither pleaded nor proved it, so the presumption was unavailable and the fee was void and unenforceable on that record. In Del Monte Properties and Investments, Inc. v. Dolan (2018) 26 Cal.App.5th Supp. 20, the appellate division stated the same allocation directly: the proponent of a liquidated damages provision in a residential lease bears the burden of proving its validity under section 1671. Neither decision holds that residential late fees are categorically void; each turned on a failure of proof by the party seeking to enforce the charge.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Appellant’s second contention is that even if such fees are allowed, the landlord must plead and prove that such damages were impracticable or extremely difficult to fix, which respondent did not do in this case."
  — Orozco v. Casimiro (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th Supp. 7, Appellate Division, Superior Court, Los Angeles County — the tenant's pleading-and-proof contention (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/7428089/orozco-v-casimiro/)
  "Once the landlord shows that it was impracticable or extremely difficult to fix actual damages, the amount the parties agreed upon is presumed to represent the amount of damage suffered by the breach."
  — Orozco v. Casimiro (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th Supp. 7, the presumption that follows a successful impracticability showing (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/7428089/orozco-v-casimiro/)
  "Respondent’s complaint did not plead that the late fee was impracticable or extremely difficult to fix. Furthermore, respondent did not present any such evidence at trial."
  — Orozco v. Casimiro (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th Supp. 7, the consequence of no pleading and no evidence (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/7428089/orozco-v-casimiro/)
  "In the absence of such evidence, he was not entitled to the presumption that the late fee was the amount of damage caused by the late payment. Thus, under the evidence in this case, the late fee was void and unenforceable."
  — Orozco v. Casimiro (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th Supp. 7, the holding on that record (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/7428089/orozco-v-casimiro/)
  "The proponent of a liquidated damages provision in a residential lease bears the burden of proving its validity under Civil Code §1671."
  — Del Monte Properties and Investments, Inc. v. Dolan (2018) 26 Cal.App.5th Supp. 20, Appellate Division, Superior Court, Humboldt County — allocation of the burden (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4527803/del-monte-properties-and-investments-inc-v-dolan/)
  Known gap: Orozco and Del Monte are opinions of the appellate divisions of the Los Angeles and Humboldt County superior courts, published in the Official Reports. Under California practice a published appellate division opinion is citable and binds the trial courts within its own appellate district but is not binding on the Courts of Appeal or on appellate divisions elsewhere; no California Court of Appeal or Supreme Court decision applying section 1671(d) specifically to a residential rent late fee was located in this research, and California Rules of Court, rule 8.1115 and rule 8.1000 et seq. were not fetched. The Del Monte text quoted here is the appellate division's May 11, 2018 ruling and decision as posted by CourtListener, bearing the notation "Filed 5/11/18; Supreme Court publication order 8/8/18"; the Official Reports pagination was not independently consulted. Orozco was decided under the same 1977 text of section 1671 quoted in this sheet. This sheet does not state whether any late fee at 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 was pleaded or proved in any proceeding.

THE TWO ELEMENTS A LATE FEE MUST SATISFY: IMPRACTICABILITY AND A REASONABLE ENDEAVOR
California courts describe section 1671(d) as imposing two requirements, and the absence of either makes the provision void. First, it must have been impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage. Second, the agreed amount must represent the result of a reasonable endeavor by the parties to estimate a fair average compensation for the loss that may be sustained. Orozco stated both requirements in quoting Hitz v. First Interstate Bank (1995) 38 Cal.App.4th 274, and added that absent either element the provision is void although the breaching party remains liable for the actual damages resulting from the breach. Del Monte applied the second element to a residential late fee and identified three things that cut against it: setting the charge as a percentage of the contract price, which the court said demonstrates a purpose other than compensating losses; the absence of any analysis of actual losses before the amount was set; and after-the-fact justification, which the court said will be rejected.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Additionally, “the amount of liquidated damages ‘must represent the result of a reasonable endeavor by the parties to estimate a fair average compensation for any loss that may be sustained.’ [Citation.]” (Ibid.) Finally, “[a]bsent either of these elements, a liquidated damages provision is void, although breaching parties remain liable for the actual damages resulting from the breach. [Citation.]”"
  — Orozco v. Casimiro (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th Supp. 7, the reasonable-endeavor element and the effect of failing either element (quoting Hitz v. First Interstate Bank) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/7428089/orozco-v-casimiro/)
  "To be valid under Civil Code §1671, a liquidated damages clause must be the result of a reasonable endeavor to approximate actual losses caused by the breach being compensated. ... Setting the liquidated damages to a percentage of the contract price demonstrates a purpose other than compensating losses. ... Some analysis of actual losses is required prior to setting the amount. ... Post-hoc rationalization will be rejected."
  — Del Monte Properties and Investments, Inc. v. Dolan (2018) 26 Cal.App.5th Supp. 20, the reasonable-endeavor requirement, percentage pricing, prior analysis, and post-hoc rationalization (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4527803/del-monte-properties-and-investments-inc-v-dolan/)
  Known gap: The two-element formulation quoted from Orozco is Orozco's own quotation of Hitz v. First Interstate Bank (1995) 38 Cal.App.4th 274, a credit-card late-fee case arising under section 1671(c)(1) rather than a lease; Hitz itself was not fetched for this sheet, and the quoted words are verified only as they appear in the Orozco opinion text, including Orozco's internal quotation marks and "[Citation.]" markers. The Del Monte propositions quoted here rest in that opinion on In re Cellphone Termination Fee Cases (2011) 193 Cal.App.4th 298, Garrett v. Coast & Southern Fed. Sav. & Loan Assn. (1973) 9 Cal.3d 731, and Util. Consumers' Action Network, Inc. v. AT&T Broadband of Southern California, Inc. (2006) 135 Cal.App.4th 1023; of those, only Garrett was independently fetched. Neither opinion states a percentage or dollar amount that would satisfy or fail the test, and this sheet states none.

A RECITAL IN THE LEASE THAT DAMAGES ARE HARD TO FIX IS NOT ITSELF PROOF
Residential leases commonly recite that late payment will cause the landlord costs whose exact amount is extremely difficult and impractical to determine, and that the stated charge is a fair and reasonable estimate of those costs. Del Monte addressed a lease containing exactly such a recital and held that the recital did not settle the question: courts look beyond the language of the contract to determine the actual circumstances of a liquidated damages clause, and agreement to an invalid liquidated damages clause does not insulate it from attack under section 1671. The court also found the landlord's trial testimony insufficient because it was little more than a reference to the language of the lease and did not articulate specific facts about the circumstances of the case. The same principle appears in the Supreme Court's earlier analysis in Garrett, which asked what the parties actually did rather than what the contract said.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Courts look beyond the language of the contract to determine the actual circumstances of a liquidated damages clause. ... Agreement to an invalid liquidated damages clause does not insulate it from attack under Civil Code §1671."
  — Del Monte Properties and Investments, Inc. v. Dolan (2018) 26 Cal.App.5th Supp. 20, looking beyond the contract language; agreement does not insulate an invalid clause (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4527803/del-monte-properties-and-investments-inc-v-dolan/)
  "At trial, Respondent testified about types of losses caused by late payment of rent, but this was little more than a reference to the language of the lease. Respondent did not articulate specific facts showing why the circumstances of this case justify liquidated damages to compensate losses caused by late payment."
  — Del Monte Properties and Investments, Inc. v. Dolan (2018) 26 Cal.App.5th Supp. 20, testimony that merely tracked the lease language (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4527803/del-monte-properties-and-investments-inc-v-dolan/)
  Known gap: Del Monte's statement that courts look beyond the contract language is supported in that opinion by a citation to Garrett v. Coast & Southern Fed. Sav. & Loan Assn. (1973) 9 Cal.3d 731, 737; the sentence about agreement not insulating an invalid clause carries no citation in the opinion text. The lease recital described in the first sentence of this clause is a summary of the lease term quoted in the Del Monte opinion (a $50 late charge after a five-day grace period), not a statement that any particular form of lease, or any agreement concerning 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814, contains that language. Whether a recital plus actual supporting evidence would suffice was not decided; Del Monte turned on the evidence actually offered.

THE PENALTY PRINCIPLE: GARRETT V. COAST & SOUTHERN FEDERAL SAVINGS & LOAN ASSN.
The California Supreme Court's leading decision on late charges is Garrett v. Coast & Southern Federal Sav. & Loan Assn. (1973) 9 Cal.3d 731, a case about late charges on home loan installments rather than rent. Garrett said that whether a late charge represents a reasonable endeavor to estimate fair compensation depends on the motivation and purpose in imposing the charge and on its effect, and that if the sum is designed to substantially exceed the damages suffered, the charge — whatever its label — is an invalid attempt to impose a penalty because its primary purpose is to compel prompt payment by threatening charges bearing little or no relationship to the actual loss. Applying that reasoning, the court held a late charge measured against the unpaid balance of the loan to be punitive in character. Garrett also made clear that the outcome is evidentiary rather than categorical: if the test of impracticability is met, a court should give effect to a liquidated damages provision that resulted from the parties' reasonable endeavors to fix fair compensation. Later residential-lease decisions, including Orozco and Del Monte, cite Garrett for these propositions.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Whether late charges represent a reasonable endeavor to estimate fair compensation depends upon the motivation and purpose in imposing such charges and their effect. If the sum extracted from the borrower is designed to exceed substantially the damages suffered by the lender, the provision for the additional sum, whatever its label, is an invalid attempt to impose a penalty inasmuch as its primary purpose is to compel prompt payment through the threat of imposition of charges bearing little or no relationship to the amount of the actual loss incurred by the lender."
  — Garrett v. Coast & Southern Federal Sav. & Loan Assn. (1973) 9 Cal.3d 731, California Supreme Court — when a late charge is a penalty (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1183486/garrett-v-coast-southern-federal-savings-loan-assn/)
  "We are compelled to conclude that a charge for the late payment of a loan installment which is measured against the unpaid balance of the loan must be deemed to be punitive in character. It is an attempt to coerce timely payment by a forfeiture which is not reasonably calculated to merely compensate the injured lender."
  — Garrett v. Coast & Southern Federal Sav. & Loan Assn. (1973) 9 Cal.3d 731, a charge measured against the unpaid balance held punitive (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1183486/garrett-v-coast-southern-federal-savings-loan-assn/)
  "If the test of impracticability is met the court should give effect to a liquidated damages provision resulting from the reasonable endeavors of the parties to fix a fair compensation."
  — Garrett v. Coast & Southern Federal Sav. & Loan Assn. (1973) 9 Cal.3d 731, a valid provision is still possible if the test is met (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1183486/garrett-v-coast-southern-federal-savings-loan-assn/)
  Known gap: Garrett was decided in 1973 and construed the then-existing Civil Code sections 1670 and 1671, which were repealed and replaced by the present sections 1671 through 1681 in 1977 (Stats. 1977, Ch. 198); the 1977 legislation and its legislative history were not fetched, and this clause does not assert that Garrett's framework carried over unchanged by force of the statute itself — it is cited because the later residential-lease opinions quoted elsewhere in this sheet rely on it. Garrett concerned a loan secured by real property, not a lease, and the words "lender" and "borrower" in the quoted passages are the court's. The Garrett opinion text on CourtListener contains scanning defects elsewhere in the opinion (for example "hable" for "liable"); the passages quoted here were checked to be free of such defects, and no passage containing one is quoted.

WHAT A LANDLORD'S ACTUAL LOSS FROM LATE RENT CONSISTS OF
Because a void liquidated damages clause leaves the breaching party liable for actual damages, the content of a landlord's actual loss from late rent matters. Orozco rejected the argument that a landlord's loss is limited to interest, stating that a landlord is not limited to interest as damages as a consequence of the late payment of money and is also entitled to administrative costs reasonably related to collecting and accounting for late payments. Del Monte stated the same measure from the other direction: the losses caused by late payment of residential rent are limited to interest and administrative costs of collecting and accounting for the late rent. Garrett described the equivalent measure for a lender as the period of time the money was wrongfully withheld plus the administrative costs reasonably related to collecting and accounting for a late payment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "A landlord is not limited to interest as damages as a consequence of the late payment of money."
  — Orozco v. Casimiro (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th Supp. 7, a landlord's damages are not limited to interest (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/7428089/orozco-v-casimiro/)
  "The losses caused by late payment of residential rent are limited to interest and administrative costs of collecting and accounting for the late rent."
  — Del Monte Properties and Investments, Inc. v. Dolan (2018) 26 Cal.App.5th Supp. 20, the outer limit of the loss caused by late rent (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4527803/del-monte-properties-and-investments-inc-v-dolan/)
  "The lender’s charges could be fairly measured by the period of time the money was wrongfully withheld plus the administrative costs reasonably related to collecting and accounting for a late payment."
  — Garrett v. Coast & Southern Federal Sav. & Loan Assn. (1973) 9 Cal.3d 731, the components of the actual loss from a late payment (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1183486/garrett-v-coast-southern-federal-savings-loan-assn/)
  Known gap: The phrase "administrative costs reasonably related to collecting and accounting for" appears in the Orozco opinion inside nested quotation marks attributing it to Hitz v. First Interstate Bank (1995) 38 Cal.App.4th 274, 278, itself quoting Beasley v. Wells Fargo Bank (1991) 235 Cal.App.3d 1383, 1390; the CourtListener rendering of those nested marks is typographically garbled in both copies fetched, so this clause quotes only the surrounding sentence that is free of the garbling and paraphrases the nested phrase in the body rather than presenting it as a quotation. Neither opinion quantifies interest or administrative costs or states a method for calculating them, and this sheet states none. The Garrett sentence describing the lender's measure appears in a passage that also contains the scanning defect "hable" for "liable"; that sentence is quoted here from the portion free of the defect, and the preceding sentence is not quoted.

CALIFORNIA SETS NO DOLLAR OR PERCENTAGE CEILING ON A RESIDENTIAL RENT LATE FEE
Section 1671 states a standard, not a number. It contains no dollar cap, no percentage of monthly rent, and no minimum grace period for a residential late fee, and no other California statute located in this research fixes such an amount for residential rent generally. Section 1671(a) contemplates that a different statute may displace it, providing that section 1671 does not apply where another statute expressly applicable to the contract prescribes the rules or standard for determining the validity of a liquidated damages provision. The Legislature has fixed a late-charge ceiling in at least one neighboring context: for a delinquent assessment in a common interest development, Civil Code section 5650(b)(2) permits a late charge not exceeding 10 percent of the delinquent assessment or ten dollars, whichever is greater, and less if the declaration so specifies. No comparable provision appears in the statutes governing residential rent.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "This section does not apply in any case where another statute expressly applicable to the contract prescribes the rules or standard for determining the validity of a provision in the contract liquidating the damages for the breach of the contract."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1671(a), California Civil Code, deference to an expressly applicable statute (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1671.)
  "A late charge not exceeding 10 percent of the delinquent assessment or ten dollars ($10), whichever is greater, unless the declaration specifies a late charge in a smaller amount, in which case any late charge imposed shall not exceed the amount specified in the declaration."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 5650(b)(2), California Civil Code, an express late-charge ceiling for common interest development assessments (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=5650.)
  Known gap: This clause states the absence of a general statutory ceiling based on the text of section 1671 and on a search of the corpus's sources; it is a negative finding, and a local rent-stabilization ordinance, a housing-program regulation, or a lease-specific statute not fetched here could impose limits that section 1671(a) would then make controlling. No city or county ordinance was fetched, and none is cited. Civil Code section 5650 governs assessments owed to a common interest development association by an owner, not rent owed by a tenant; it is quoted only as a contrast showing what an express statutory late-charge ceiling looks like, and the corpus's separate HOA assessment lien and foreclosure information sheet covers section 5650 in its own context. Whether any charge at 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 falls under an expressly applicable statute within the meaning of section 1671(a) is not addressed.

LATE FEES, THE THREE-DAY NOTICE FOR NONPAYMENT, AND FEES FOR SERVING NOTICES
A three-day notice for nonpayment of rent under Code of Civil Procedure section 1161(2) must state the amount that is due, along with the name, telephone number, and address of the person to whom the rent is to be paid and, where payment may be made in person, the usual days and hours that person is available. Del Monte connected the late-fee question to that requirement: it stated that a defective notice is fatal to an unlawful detainer complaint, citing Wasatch Property Management v. Degrate (2005) 35 Cal.4th 1111, and held the notice before it defective because it may include an invalid late fee and may not support a judgment for unlawful detainer — the notice there had demanded $600 in rent plus a $50 late fee as a single $650 total. Separately, section 1161(6) provides that a landlord or its agent shall not charge a tenant a fee for serving, posting, or otherwise delivering any notice described in that section.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "after default in the payment of rent, pursuant to the lease or agreement under which the property is held, and three days’ notice, excluding Saturdays and Sundays and other judicial holidays, in writing, requiring its payment, stating the amount that is due, the name, telephone number, and address of the person to whom the rent payment shall be made, and, if payment may be made personally, the usual days and hours that person will be available to receive the payment"
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161(2), California Code of Civil Procedure, required contents of a three-day notice for nonpayment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1161.)
  "It is settled law that a defective notice is fatal to an unlawful detainer complaint. ... The notice upon which the complaint in this case is based is defective because it may include an invalid late fee and it may not support a judgment for unlawful detainer."
  — Del Monte Properties and Investments, Inc. v. Dolan (2018) 26 Cal.App.5th Supp. 20, a defective notice and an invalid late fee (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4527803/del-monte-properties-and-investments-inc-v-dolan/)
  "A landlord or its agent shall not charge a tenant a fee for serving, posting, or otherwise delivering any notice, as described in this section."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1161(6), California Code of Civil Procedure, no fee for serving a notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1161.)
  Known gap: Wasatch Property Management v. Degrate (2005) 35 Cal.4th 1111 was not fetched; it is named only as the authority Del Monte cited, in Del Monte's own words. Del Monte's holding is phrased in the permissive "may include an invalid late fee and it may not support a judgment," and this clause reproduces that phrasing rather than restating it as a categorical rule that any notice mentioning a late fee is void. Whether a late fee can ever be "rent" that is properly demanded in a section 1161(2) notice was not resolved by the text fetched, and no case deciding that question was fetched. Section 1161 as quoted is the current text on the California Legislative Information site; the amendment history of subdivision (6) was not traced. This clause does not evaluate any notice served at 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814.

A SEPARATE STATUTE FOR DISHONORED CHECKS: CIVIL CODE SECTION 1719
A charge for a rent check that does not clear is governed by its own statute rather than by the liquidated damages analysis. Civil Code section 1719(a)(1) makes a person who passes a check on insufficient funds liable to the payee for the amount of the check plus a service charge not exceeding twenty-five dollars for the first such check and not exceeding thirty-five dollars for each subsequent check to that payee. Section 1719(a)(2) provides for treble damages, of not less than one hundred dollars and not more than one thousand five hundred dollars, if the payee mails a statutory written demand by certified mail and the drawer does not pay within thirty days. Section 1719(a)(3) withholds the service charge, mailing costs, and treble damages where the drawer stopped payment to resolve a good faith dispute with the payee, and places on the payee the burden of proving by clear and convincing evidence that there was no good faith dispute. Section 1719(a)(6) defines passing a check on insufficient funds to include a check the drawee refuses to honor because of lack of funds, because the writer has no account there, or because the writer stopped payment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-13]
  "Notwithstanding any penal sanctions that may apply, any person who passes a check on insufficient funds shall be liable to the payee for the amount of the check and a service charge payable to the payee for an amount not to exceed twenty-five dollars ($25) for the first check passed on insufficient funds and an amount not to exceed thirty-five dollars ($35) for each subsequent check to that payee passed on insufficient funds."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1719(a)(1), California Civil Code, the insufficient-funds service charge (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1719.)
  "The person who had passed a check on insufficient funds shall have 30 days from the date the written demand was mailed to pay the amount of the check, the amount of the service charge payable to the payee, and the costs to mail the written demand for payment. ... and damages equal to treble that amount, which shall not be less than one hundred dollars ($100) nor more than one thousand five hundred dollars ($1,500)."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1719(a)(2), California Civil Code, treble damages after a certified-mail written demand (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1719.)
  "Notwithstanding paragraphs (1) and (2), a person shall not be liable for the service charge, costs to mail the written demand, or treble damages if he or she stops payment in order to resolve a good faith dispute with the payee. The payee is entitled to the service charge, costs to mail the written demand, or treble damages only upon proving by clear and convincing evidence that there was no good faith dispute, as defined in subdivision (b)."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1719(a)(3), California Civil Code, the good faith dispute exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1719.)
  "(A) Lack of funds or credit in the account to pay the check. (B) The person who wrote the check does not have an account with the drawee. (C) The person who wrote the check instructed the drawee to stop payment on the check."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1719(a)(6), California Civil Code, what it means to pass a check on insufficient funds (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1719.)
  Known gap: Section 1719 speaks of a "payee" and applies to checks generally; it is not limited to rent, and its text does not mention landlords, tenants, or leases. This clause does not state whether a returned-check or "NSF" charge written into a lease is analyzed under section 1719, under section 1671(d), or under both — the Del Monte lease quoted in that opinion set its NSF fees at the section 1719 amounts, but the opinion decided only the late-fee question and no fetched authority resolves the relationship between the two statutes. The good-faith-dispute provision in subdivision (a)(3) is tied to a stop payment; subdivision (a)(4) and (a)(5) contain separate exceptions for bank error and for delayed direct deposit of a government benefit, which are summarized nowhere in this sheet. expectedJSON.body: This information sheet describes how California law treats a late fee charged on residential rent — a contractual charge a tenant owes when rent is paid after its due date — as it may bear on the tenancy of Jordan Lee at 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 under a rental agreement with Pat Morgan. It states what Civil Code sections 1671 and 1951.5 provide, what California courts have said about when such a charge is enforceable and when it is a void penalty, what a landlord may recover as actual damages when a late-fee clause is void, what Code of Civil Procedure section 1161 requires a three-day notice for nonpayment to state, and what Civil Code section 1719 provides about a service charge on a dishonored check. It does not determine whether any particular late fee, rental agreement term, or notice concerning 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 is valid, and it does not tell Pat Morgan or Jordan Lee what to do about any charge or dispute.

A late fee in a residential rental agreement is a contractual provision fixing in advance what the tenant owes for a breach — paying rent late — so California's liquidated damages statute governs it. Civil Code section 1951.5 states that section 1671, relating to liquidated damages, applies to a lease of real property. Section 1671 then divides liquidated damages provisions into two tracks. Under subdivision (b), the general rule for contracts is that such a provision is valid unless the party attacking it shows it was unreasonable when the contract was made. Subdivision (c)(2) removes a lease of real property for use as a dwelling by the tenant, or by those dependent on the tenant for support, from that general rule: for such a lease, validity is determined under subdivision (d) and not under subdivision (b). Subdivision (d) states that in those cases the provision is void, except that the parties may agree on an amount presumed to be the damage sustained by the breach when, from the nature of the case, it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage. The statutory default for a dwelling lease is therefore the opposite of the general contract default: the clause is void unless the impracticability condition is satisfied, rather than valid unless shown unreasonable.

expectedJSON.body: Two published California appellate division decisions have applied section 1671(d) to a residential late fee, and both placed the burden on the landlord. In Orozco v. Casimiro (2004) 121 Cal.App.4th Supp. 7, a landlord's unlawful detainer case rested on a $50 late fee in a lease. The court described the tenant's contention as being that the landlord must plead and prove that damages were impracticable or extremely difficult to fix. It held that once a landlord makes that showing, the agreed amount is presumed to represent the damage suffered — but the landlord there had neither pleaded nor proved it, so the presumption was unavailable and the fee was void and unenforceable on that record. In Del Monte Properties and Investments, Inc. v. Dolan (2018) 26 Cal.App.5th Supp. 20, the appellate division stated the same allocation directly: the proponent of a liquidated damages provision in a residential lease bears the burden of proving its validity under section 1671. Neither decision holds that residential late fees are categorically void; each turned on a failure of proof by the party seeking to enforce the charge.

expectedJSON.body: California courts describe section 1671(d) as imposing two requirements, and the absence of either makes the provision void. First, it must have been impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage. Second, the agreed amount must represent the result of a reasonable endeavor by the parties to estimate a fair average compensation for the loss that may be sustained. Orozco stated both requirements in quoting Hitz v. First Interstate Bank (1995) 38 Cal.App.4th 274, and added that absent either element the provision is void although the breaching party remains liable for the actual damages resulting from the breach. Del Monte applied the second element to a residential late fee and identified three things that cut against it: setting the charge as a percentage of the contract price, which the court said demonstrates a purpose other than compensating losses; the absence of any analysis of actual losses before the amount was set; and after-the-fact justification, which the court said will be rejected.

citations.quote: Additionally, “the amount of liquidated damages ‘must represent the result of a reasonable endeavor by the parties to estimate a fair average compensation for any loss that may be sustained.’ [Citation.]” (Ibid.) Finally, “[a]bsent either of these elements, a liquidated damages provision is void, although breaching parties remain liable for the actual damages resulting from the breach. [Citation.]”

citations.case: Del Monte Properties and Investments, Inc. v. Dolan (2018) 26 Cal.App.5th Supp. 20
citations.cite: the reasonable-endeavor requirement, percentage pricing, prior analysis, and post-hoc rationalization
citations.quote: To be valid under Civil Code §1671, a liquidated damages clause must be the result of a reasonable endeavor to approximate actual losses caused by the breach being compensated. ... Setting the liquidated damages to a percentage of the contract price demonstrates a purpose other than compensating losses. ... Some analysis of actual losses is required prior to setting the amount. ... Post-hoc rationalization will be rejected.

expectedJSON.body: Residential leases commonly recite that late payment will cause the landlord costs whose exact amount is extremely difficult and impractical to determine, and that the stated charge is a fair and reasonable estimate of those costs. Del Monte addressed a lease containing exactly such a recital and held that the recital did not settle the question: courts look beyond the language of the contract to determine the actual circumstances of a liquidated damages clause, and agreement to an invalid liquidated damages clause does not insulate it from attack under section 1671. The court also found the landlord's trial testimony insufficient because it was little more than a reference to the language of the lease and did not articulate specific facts about the circumstances of the case. The same principle appears in the Supreme Court's earlier analysis in Garrett, which asked what the parties actually did rather than what the contract said.

expectedJSON.body: The California Supreme Court's leading decision on late charges is Garrett v. Coast & Southern Federal Sav. & Loan Assn. (1973) 9 Cal.3d 731, a case about late charges on home loan installments rather than rent. Garrett said that whether a late charge represents a reasonable endeavor to estimate fair compensation depends on the motivation and purpose in imposing the charge and on its effect, and that if the sum is designed to substantially exceed the damages suffered, the charge — whatever its label — is an invalid attempt to impose a penalty because its primary purpose is to compel prompt payment by threatening charges bearing little or no relationship to the actual loss. Applying that reasoning, the court held a late charge measured against the unpaid balance of the loan to be punitive in character. Garrett also made clear that the outcome is evidentiary rather than categorical: if the test of impracticability is met, a court should give effect to a liquidated damages provision that resulted from the parties' reasonable endeavors to fix fair compensation. Later residential-lease decisions, including Orozco and Del Monte, cite Garrett for these propositions.

citations.quote: Whether late charges represent a reasonable endeavor to estimate fair compensation depends upon the motivation and purpose in imposing such charges and their effect. If the sum extracted from the borrower is designed to exceed substantially the damages suffered by the lender, the provision for the additional sum, whatever its label, is an invalid attempt to impose a penalty inasmuch as its primary purpose is to compel prompt payment through the threat of imposition of charges bearing little or no relationship to the amount of the actual loss incurred by the lender.

It is an attempt to coerce timely payment by a forfeiture which is not reasonably calculated to merely compensate the injured lender.

expectedJSON.body: Because a void liquidated damages clause leaves the breaching party liable for actual damages, the content of a landlord's actual loss from late rent matters. Orozco rejected the argument that a landlord's loss is limited to interest, stating that a landlord is not limited to interest as damages as a consequence of the late payment of money and is also entitled to administrative costs reasonably related to collecting and accounting for late payments. Del Monte stated the same measure from the other direction: the losses caused by late payment of residential rent are limited to interest and administrative costs of collecting and accounting for the late rent. Garrett described the equivalent measure for a lender as the period of time the money was wrongfully withheld plus the administrative costs reasonably related to collecting and accounting for a late payment.

expectedJSON.body: Section 1671 states a standard, not a number. It contains no dollar cap, no percentage of monthly rent, and no minimum grace period for a residential late fee, and no other California statute located in this research fixes such an amount for residential rent generally. Section 1671(a) contemplates that a different statute may displace it, providing that section 1671 does not apply where another statute expressly applicable to the contract prescribes the rules or standard for determining the validity of a liquidated damages provision. The Legislature has fixed a late-charge ceiling in at least one neighboring context: for a delinquent assessment in a common interest development, Civil Code section 5650(b)(2) permits a late charge not exceeding 10 percent of the delinquent assessment or ten dollars, whichever is greater, and less if the declaration so specifies. No comparable provision appears in the statutes governing residential rent.

expectedJSON.body: A three-day notice for nonpayment of rent under Code of Civil Procedure section 1161(2) must state the amount that is due, along with the name, telephone number, and address of the person to whom the rent is to be paid and, where payment may be made in person, the usual days and hours that person is available. Del Monte connected the late-fee question to that requirement: it stated that a defective notice is fatal to an unlawful detainer complaint, citing Wasatch Property Management v. Degrate (2005) 35 Cal.4th 1111, and held the notice before it defective because it may include an invalid late fee and may not support a judgment for unlawful detainer — the notice there had demanded $600 in rent plus a $50 late fee as a single $650 total. Separately, section 1161(6) provides that a landlord or its agent shall not charge a tenant a fee for serving, posting, or otherwise delivering any notice described in that section.

expectedJSON.body: A charge for a rent check that does not clear is governed by its own statute rather than by the liquidated damages analysis. Civil Code section 1719(a)(1) makes a person who passes a check on insufficient funds liable to the payee for the amount of the check plus a service charge not exceeding twenty-five dollars for the first such check and not exceeding thirty-five dollars for each subsequent check to that payee. Section 1719(a)(2) provides for treble damages, of not less than one hundred dollars and not more than one thousand five hundred dollars, if the payee mails a statutory written demand by certified mail and the drawer does not pay within thirty days. Section 1719(a)(3) withholds the service charge, mailing costs, and treble damages where the drawer stopped payment to resolve a good faith dispute with the payee, and places on the payee the burden of proving by clear and convincing evidence that there was no good faith dispute. Section 1719(a)(6) defines passing a check on insufficient funds to include a check the drawee refuses to honor because of lack of funds, because the writer has no account there, or because the writer stopped payment.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the insufficient-funds service charge
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any penal sanctions that may apply, any person who passes a check on insufficient funds shall be liable to the payee for the amount of the check and a service charge payable to the payee for an amount not to exceed twenty-five dollars ($25) for the first check passed on insufficient funds and an amount not to exceed thirty-five dollars ($35) for each subsequent check to that payee passed on insufficient funds.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, treble damages after a certified-mail written demand
citations.quote: The person who had passed a check on insufficient funds shall have 30 days from the date the written demand was mailed to pay the amount of the check, the amount of the service charge payable to the payee, and the costs to mail the written demand for payment. ... and damages equal to treble that amount, which shall not be less than one hundred dollars ($100) nor more than one thousand five hundred dollars ($1,500).

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the good faith dispute exception
citations.quote: Notwithstanding paragraphs (1) and (2), a person shall not be liable for the service charge, costs to mail the written demand, or treble damages if he or she stops payment in order to resolve a good faith dispute with the payee. The payee is entitled to the service charge, costs to mail the written demand, or treble damages only upon proving by clear and convincing evidence that there was no good faith dispute, as defined in subdivision (b).

citations.quote: (A) Lack of funds or credit in the account to pay the check. (B) The person who wrote the check does not have an account with the drawee. (C) The person who wrote the check instructed the drawee to stop payment on the check.
